items.title: EDGE AI: Intelligent Computing At The Edge for Real-Time Applications — A Review of Architectures, Model Optimization and Deployment
items.summary: Edge Artificial Intelligence (Edge AI) combines machine learning with edge computing so that data are processed on or near the devices that produce them, such as sensors, cameras, smartphones, IoT nodes and embedded systems, rather than entirely in remote cloud servers. This brings decisions closer to the data source, reducing latency, bandwidth use and dependence on connectivity while improving privacy. This paper reviews the foundations and practice of Edge AI for real-time applications. It examines the edge computing paradigm and edge intelligence levels, the partitioning of neural networks between device, edge server and cloud, efficient architectures such as depthwise-separable networks, early-exit inference, and compression by pruning, quantization and knowledge distillation. Tiny machine learning on microcontrollers and standard benchmarks for measuring edge inference are discussed. Applications in smart surveillance, industrial monitoring, healthcare wearables, autonomous robots and smart cities are summarized. A layered device–edge–cloud architecture is proposed, together with research gaps, objectives, a comparison of deployment tiers and an analysis of challenges including limited resources, heterogeneity, security and model updates. The review concludes that Edge AI is essential for low-latency, private and reliable intelligent systems.

items.title: CodeQuant2: Enhanced Outlier Mitigation and Adaptive Clustering for Low-Precision LRMs
items.summary: Large reasoning models (LRMs) improve task performance by generating longer intermediate reasoning traces, but this substantially increases inference costs and makes low-precision quantization increasingly important. However, aggressively quantized models often perform poorly on reasoning tasks. We observe larger activation fluctuations during the first decoding steps of reasoning. Calibration that omits these early states may miss their activation fluctuations. To address these reasoning-specific quantization challenges, we propose \textbf{CodeQuant2}, a clustering-based LUT quantization framework for low-precision large reasoning models. CodeQuant2 mitigates activation outliers with rotation and scaling, uses clustering to represent non-uniform weight distributions, and adapts codebook sizes to the quantization difficulty of each layer. Guided by our observation of reasoning-time activation behavior, CodeQuant2 further improves calibration sample selection to better match actual decoding statistics. Combined with our customized LUT CUDA kernel, CodeQuant2 delivers substantial accuracy improvements on reasoning benchmarks while achieving up to $2.85\times$ speedup over BF16.

items.title: Grasp-TAGS: Task-Aware Grasp Selection via Critic Distillation for Prehensile Loco-Manipulation
items.summary: Loco-manipulation, which requires mobile manipulators to coordinate locomotion and manipulation over long horizons, is a key capability for large-object rearrangement in applications such as service robotics and warehouse automation. Despite recent progress, reliably executing these tasks remains challenging because performance depends on complex robot-object and object-environment interaction dynamics. Existing approaches address this challenge either through model-based methods, which often require accurate dynamics models, or through learning-based methods, which reduce this requirement but typically assume a fixed or predefined initial grasp. However, different geometrically stable grasps can lead to substantially different downstream manipulation performance. items.title: Adaptive error management for fault-tolerant quantum computing across hardware-level suppression, system-level diagnosis, and real-time decoding
items.summary: Abstract Fault-tolerant quantum computing reached a milestone in December 2024 when Google’s Willow processor demonstrated below-threshold error correction on a superconducting chip, a result since reproduced on neutral-atom and alternative superconducting platforms. Yet the classical decoders needed to sustain this performance face a scaling challenge: noise becomes increasingly structured and correlated as systems grow, while decoders must respond within microsecond coherence windows. This survey asks whether error suppression, noise diagnosis, and decoding are better treated as one adaptive control problem than as three separate research programs. Drawing on a scoping review of 146 records, it organizes the field into a three-layer taxonomy. Layer 1 (Hardware-Level Suppression) integrates protection into the physical substrate; bosonic cat qubits exponentially suppress bit-flip errors, projecting up to 90% overhead reduction versus surface codes. Layer 2 (Diagnosis) employs probabilistic models and computational intelligence to characterize error sources; neuro-fuzzy architectures and the Bias–Entropy decomposition separate hardware drift from logical faults, subject to an identifiability limit that we characterize. items.title: Circuit Theory-Informed AI for Condition Monitoring in Power Electronics
items.summary: Artificial intelligence for power electronics is evolving toward a deeper comprehension of system intrinsic behaviors and dynamics. As a novel integration of neural computation and electric circuits, spike-based neuromorphic computing offers promising potential in high energy efficiency and adaptability for data-driven applications. Building on the latency-coding principles, this article proposes a framework for data-light condition monitoring that relies solely on three-phase AC current measurements. The AC current signals are encoded as membrane potentials of RC-based spiking neurons, which are inherently compatible with spiking neural networks that can effectively facilitate the estimation of device parameters. Case studies are presented to validate the performances, while constraints and further optimizations are also evaluated and discussed, and future extensions of the methodology are provided.

items.title: Neuromorphic Computing and Neuromorphic Hardware for AutoML in Zero-touch Networks: Applications and Challenges
items.summary: Owing to the fact that future communication systems are increasing in size and complexity, Zero Touch Networks (ZTN) is going toward pervasive networks that self-configure, self-optimize, and even self-heal with minimal human action. AutoML plays a crucial role in ZTN for adaptive model selection, hyperparameter tuning and real-time decision-making under dynamic network conditions. However, the latency and energy consumption of traditional cloud-based AutoML systems at edge devices are usually not acceptable. Recently, neuromorphic computing and hardware which are based on the human brain structure and function has become a promising alternative for large scale VLSI implementation because it possesses event driven processing, extremely large scale parallelism, ultra-low power consumption. We study in this paper the integration of neuromorphic computing paradigms for ZTN in AutoML. We explore how Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) and neuromorphic accelerators can enable real-time learning, adaptive control and anomaly detection in ZTNs. Core use cases such as self-heal network, 240 intelligent traffic optimization, predictive maintenance and edge driven autonomous orchestration are also considered. items.title: Innateness is (still) an orienting principle for language development
items.summary: How humans come to acquire language has been a persistent object of philosophical and scientific inquiry, in part because it bears on fundamental questions about the nature of human cognition.Classically, this field of inquiry has centered innateness as a critical component of language acquisition, traditionally characterizing innate capability in terms of richly specified, biologically endowed linguistic structure, such as Universal Grammar. Contemporary theories have evolved considerably from these earlier formulations and now present several differing candidates for innateness in language. Throughout this evolution, though, questions of innateness have remained central to theories of language acquisition, even as the nature of those questions has shifted in response to new sources of evidence. In this Perspective, we consider evidence from three complementary sources of evidence—linguistic diversity, human social interaction, and language models (LMs)—that together inform the question of what children must bring to the task of language learning. We conclude by identifying desiderata for theories of language acquisition that seek to specify the nature, scope, and explanatory role of innate contributions to language development.

items.title: Evaluating LLMs on Italian through multi-prompt: the Evalita-LLM benchmark
items.summary: Abstract We present Evalita-LLM, a novel benchmark designed to evaluate Large Language Models (LLMs) on Italian tasks. The key innovation of Evalita-LLM is the use of multiple prompts for each task, which mitigates the model’s sensitivity to specific prompt formulations and ensures a robust and objective performance assessment. We propose an iterative methodology for selecting and validating multiple prompts, and metrics that capture both high performance and stability of a prompt given a set of LLMs. The resulting Evalita-LLM multi-prompt benchmark is based on ten native Italian tasks, eliminating translation issues and potential cultural biases. It includes a mix of multiple-choice and generative tasks, enabling more natural interactions with LLMs. We report experimental results from the benchmark’s development phase, along with performance statistics for several state-of-the-art LLMs. Evalita-LLM is publicly available with a leaderboard hosted on Hugging Face to support transparent evaluation and comparison of LLMs.

items.title: Market Size Forecasting for Embodied Intelligent Robots Using a Transformer–Random Forest Ensemble
items.summary: Accurate forecasting of the embodied intelligent robot (EIR) market is valuable yet difficult, because its time series are nonlinear, multi-regime, and noisy, driven by fluctuating policy support, uneven regional adoption rates, and rapid iteration of underlying robotics technologies. This paper proposes a hybrid forecasting framework that couples a Transformer encoder with a Random Forest (RF) regressor and fuses their predictions through a weighted ensemble whose combination coefficient is selected by grid search. A comprehensive market dataset spanning 2018–2026 across six regions, eight application scenarios, and six robot categories is analyzed. Lag, rolling statistic, difference, and momentum features are engineered from region-level time series to capture temporal trends and market oscillations. On a held-out 2025–2026 test period, the proposed ensemble attains the lowest MAE (7.76) and MAPE (13.63%), while the standalone Transformer attains the highest R² (0.55). The study demonstrates the complementary strengths of deep sequence modeling and tree-based regression, while documenting the key limitations that need to be addressed before deploying this prediction pipeline in real-world market planning and investment decision-making.

items.title: Learning to remember: advances in memory mechanisms for large language models
items.summary: Abstract Memory has become a central mechanism for extending large language models (LLMs) beyond fixed context windows, stateless interaction, and static parametric knowledge. This survey organizes the literature around three complementary dimensions: the life cycle of memory, the storage substrate, and the system role that memory plays in LLM-based agents, while using cognitive-science-inspired memory concepts as a lightweight conceptual motivation rather than as a separate technical contribution or implementation family. On this basis, we distinguish three mechanism families: nonparametric memory, where information is stored outside model parameters in text, graph, multimodal, or database-like structures; parametric memory, where information is stored or accessed through activations, key-value caches, learned modules, adapter-based parameterizations, or model weights; and memory for agent evolution, where stored experiences support reinforcement learning, continual learning, procedural reuse, context engineering, and agent harness design. Evaluation is treated as a separate cross-cutting component rather than as a memory mechanism. Unlike surveys that focus primarily on retrieval-augmented generation or long-context modeling, this paper emphasizes the full memory life cycle: construction, maintenance, retrieval, consolidation, forgetting, governance, and evaluation.
